implementation_notes: kotlinx.serialization derives serializers at compile time, so the projection is declared on a data class: mark fields the receiver must never see with @Transient (they need default values and are never written), or model the narrow message as its own @Serializable DTO built from the domain object, and let Json { encodeDefaults = false } omit the defaulted ones. What replaces the classic filter object is the serializer's declared shape - the wire contract is a type, and no reflection or annotation processor stands between the class and the bytes. Because an incoming field matching a @Transient property is an error by default, a DTO that must also read the producer's superset needs Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true } (the Tolerant Reader posture). Where the JVM stack is Jackson instead, @JsonView remains the equivalent and is still justified when one domain class must expose several named views without a second type.
pitfalls: @Transient from kotlinx.serialization is not kotlin.jvm.Transient: the JVM annotation compiles and the field still ships, which is a silent leak.
@Transient requires a default value, and with the default Json configuration a payload containing a property of that name fails with JsonDecodingException instead of ignoring it.
Serializing a DTO whose properties are nullable writes explicit nulls unless explicitNulls = false, so 'field absent' and 'field null' end up meaning the same thing to the receiver.
Inheritance is projected too: a DTO declared as a subclass or a sealed hierarchy needs its own polymorphic configuration, otherwise fields of the parent class travel with every view.
